title: Shutter & Motion

learn.summary: The shutter decides how time appears in a still image: frozen mid-air, streaked with energy, or smoothed into silk. Two separate blurs must be mastered — subject motion blur (creative choice) and camera shake (almost always a defect). Control both and you control time.

do: Photograph moving traffic twice this week — once freezing it, once deliberately blurring it — using your phone's manual or night mode.

children.title: Freeze or Blur

learn.summary: Rules of thumb: 1/500–1/1000 s freezes sports and pets, 1/250 handles walking people, while 1/30 and slower lets motion paint. Blur communicates speed better than sharpness — a frozen cyclist looks parked; a streaked one looks fast. Decide the story before choosing the speed.

do: Shoot someone jumping at 1/1000 and again at 1/30 — caption each frame with the feeling it conveys.

children.title: Beating Camera Shake

learn.summary: The reciprocal rule: handheld shutter speed should be at least 1/focal length (1/50 s for a 50mm lens; faster on crop sensors). Stabilization buys a few extra stops but cannot freeze a moving subject. Technique is free stabilization: elbows tucked, exhale, squeeze — or brace the phone against a wall, table, or your own knee.

do: Shoot the same dim scene handheld at 1/60, 1/15, and 1/4 second, then zoom to 100% and find your personal slowest sharp speed.

children.title: Panning

learn.summary: Panning swings the camera with a moving subject at a slow shutter (try 1/30–1/60 s for cyclists and cars): the subject stays sharp while the background streaks horizontally. Follow through after the shot like a golf swing. Expect a 1-in-10 hit rate at first — that is normal, not failure.

do: Stand by a street this week and take 20 panning shots of passing cars or bikes at 1/30 s — keep the two best.

children.title: Long Exposure

learn.summary: Exposures of a second to several minutes turn waterfalls silky, erase walking pedestrians, and pull star trails across the sky — but they demand total camera stillness, so a tripod or improvised support is non-negotiable. Phone night modes are computational long exposures already. Daylight long exposures need an ND (neutral density) filter to block excess light.

do: Prop your phone on a solid surface tonight, use night mode or a 3–10 s manual exposure on moving lights or water, and shoot five frames.
